fields.current: Should nine kinds of projects, led by housing, get an optional fast track through environmental review?

evidence.excerpt: an applicant may elect to utilize none, some, or all of the provisions of this chapter
Housing.

fields.explanation: Optional procedures and nine LAO-listed types confirmed. 'Led by housing' reflects housing being listed first.

fields.current: Nine project types (housing, water, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, schools, transportation) can opt into a faster environmental review (CEQA) with firm deadlines. Lawsuits must be filed within 30 days and decided within 270 days including appeals, which courts may extend by 90. Courts can pause only the flawed part of a project.

evidence.excerpt: Housing. Water system (not including Delta conveyance facilities). Clean energy (not including nuclear power). Health facility, clinic, and medical office building. Fire, police, and sheriff’s stations. Wildfire risk reduction. Broadband Internet access. Education facility. Transportation (not including high-speed rail).
shall be commenced within 30 days from the date the public agency files a notice of determination or notice of exemption
The action or proceeding shall be completed within 270 days, inclusive of original and appellate court proceedings,
The court may, in its own discretion, extend the 270-day deadline contained in subparagraph (A) by up to an additional 90 days.
shall only be extended upon mutual written consent of the plaintiff or petitioner
Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA

fields.explanation: Types, 30-day filing, 270-day completion, 90-day court extension and partial halt all confirmed. The text also allows further extension by mutual written consent of the parties, so '270 days ... which courts may extend by 90' is incomplete. 'Schools' is narrower than LAO's 'Education facility'.
fields.proposedText: Nine project types (housing, water, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, education facilities, transportation) can opt into a faster environmental review (CEQA) with firm deadlines. Lawsuits must be filed within 30 days and decided within 270 days including appeals. Courts may add up to 90 days, and longer only if all parties agree. Courts can pause only the flawed part of a project.
fields.limitations: LAO excludes Delta conveyance, nuclear and high-speed rail from the categories; not mentioned in our text.

fields.current: This includes ten exemptions the Legislature passed in 2025.

evidence.excerpt: Together, these bills create ten new CEQA exemptions aimed at fast-tracking housing, childcare, water infrastructure,
On June 30, 2025, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law budget trailer bills AB 130 and SB 131
as added by Section 59 of Chapter 22 of the Statutes of 2025 (Assembly Bill 130)

fields.explanation: The count of ten comes only from one independent law-firm alert; another firm lists ten categories plus a separate manufacturing exemption, and LAO/SOS do not mention 2025 exemptions. Existence of 2025 exemptions (AB 130, SB 131) is confirmed by multiple law firms.
fields.proposedText: This includes CEQA exemptions the Legislature passed in 2025.
fields.limitations: Rule 9: no official source for the count. Prop 45 text also references AB 130 for housing projects that use the new chapter, so the 2025 laws are not only a NO-side feature.

fields.current: LAO estimates initial state and local costs likely in the high tens of millions a year, possibly over $100 million, partly covered by fees. Long-term effects are uncertain.

Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs.
In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more signifcant positive or negative fscal efects for state and local governments.

fields.current: Supporters' official argument says approvals are too slow and costly for housing, water, energy, schools and hospitals, and this keeps protections.

evidence.excerpt: California’s outdated system for approving essential housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools, hospitals, and wildfire prevention projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly
Prop. 45 does not exempt a single project from environmental review.

fields.current: Opponents' official argument says it limits environmental review and public input while its funders profit.

evidence.excerpt: Proposition 45 limits both the environmental review of major new development projects and the public’s right to be heard.
The corporations paying for Prop. 45 will profit while you keep paying.

fields.current: How many projects opt in and whether housing gets built faster. There is no neutral figure for how long CEQA lawsuits take today. A study by Holland & Knight attorney Jennifer Hernandez, who helped write Prop 45, puts it at about five years.

head of Holland & Knight's West Coast Land Use and Environmental Group and lead author of the study.
Jennifer Hernandez, a Holland & Knight land-use attorney who helped write the ballot language,

fields.explanation: Holland & Knight's own release says four to five years; its report says about five. 'Helped write Prop 45' rests only on HousingWire (independent). LAO gives no duration.
fields.proposedText: How many projects opt in and whether housing gets built faster. There is no neutral figure for how long CEQA lawsuits take today. A Holland & Knight study led by Jennifer Hernandez, who HousingWire reports helped write the measure, puts it at four to five years.
fields.limitations: LAO page returned no lawsuit-length data (reader finding). Holland & Knight recommends passing Prop 45, so it is an interested source.
